Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Marie Curie is a physicist. Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
Which of these is a chemist?
Alfred Nobel is a chemist. Alfred Bernhard Nobel ( noh-BEL; Swedish: [ˈǎlːfrɛd nʊˈbɛlː]; 21 October 1833 – 10 December 1896) was a Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer, and businessman.
What is the atomic number of Fermium?
Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.
In what year was Neil Armstrong born?
Neil Armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised near Wapakoneta, Ohio.
In what year did Karl Marx die?
Karl Marx: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia, Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841.
In what year was Argon discovered?
Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.
Which company manufactures Consolidated B-24 Liberator?
Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control
Consolidated B-24 Liberator: North American Aviation. The Consolidated B-24 Liberator is an American heavy bomber, designed by Consolidated Aircraft of San Diego, California.
In which country is Virgo interferometer?
Virgo interferometer: Italy. The Virgo interferometer is a large-scale scientific instrument near Pisa, Italy, for detecting gravitational waves.
Who is credited with discovering Archaea?
Archaea: Carl Woese. Archaea (ar-KEE-ə) is a domain of organisms.
Who is credited with discovering Synapse?
Synapse: Charles Scott Sherrington. In the nervous system, a synapse is a structure that allows a neuron to exchange (receive or send) signals with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
Who is credited with discovering Nitrogen?
Nitrogen: Daniel Rutherford. Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Known by the abbreviation NAC, this mucolytic drug treats acetaminophen overdose and also loosens thick mucus in people with chronic lung conditions like pneumonia and bronchitis — which drug?

Acetylcysteine (NAC) is a mucolytic that is used to treat paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and to loosen thick mucus in individuals with chronic bronchopulmonary disorders, such as pneumonia and bronchitis.
This amphoteric compound forms a gelatinous precipitate in water and occurs naturally as the mineral gibbsite, one of bauxite's key components — what is it?
Aluminium hydroxide is a white chemical compound that is found as the mineral gibbsite (also known as hydrargillite) and its three much rarer polymorphs: bayerite, doyleite, and nordstrandite.
This lustrous grey metalloid, found mainly in the mineral stibnite, was historically powdered for use as a cosmetic known by its Arabic name, kohl. What element is it?
Antimony is a chemical element with the symbol Sb (from Latin stibium) and atomic number 51.

The third-largest member of its family behind the Siberian taimen and Pacific Chinook, this anadromous fish hatches in rivers, matures at sea, and changes color and appearance when it returns upstream to spawn — name this fish?
Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) is a species of ray-finned fish in the family Salmonidae.
Coined in 1814 by chemist William Hyde Wollaston, this polyatomic anion forms as carbonic acid loses a proton, and plays a crucial role buffering the body's pH — what's the ion?
Bicarbonate (American; nomenclature: hydrogencarbonate) is an intermediate form in the deprotonation of carbonic acid.

Making up only about 2.6 percent of the brain's total weight, this stalk-like structure connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and regulates critical functions like heart rate and breathing. What is it called?
Brainstem (or brain stem) is the posterior stalk-like part of the brain that connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord.

Standing in contrast to the 'cat-like' carnivorans that diversified across Africa and southern Asia, this suborder unites dogs, bears, raccoons, and pinnipeds under one 'dog-like' umbrella — what's it called?
Caniformia is a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of "dog-like" carnivorans.
First cultivated in Mesoamerica and later spread worldwide during the Columbian Exchange, this edible gourd-family plant is also known as christophine, mirliton, or choko — what is it?

Chayote (previously placed in the obsolete genus Sechium, now in the genus Sicyos, as Sicyos edulis), also known as christophine, mirliton, gisquil, and choko, is an edible plant belonging to the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae.
Mostly belonging to the genus Naja, these venomous snakes are known for rearing upward and flaring a distinctive hood when threatened — name this common snake type?
Cobra is the common name of various venomous snakes, most of which belong to the genus Naja.
Belonging to the same genus as poliovirus and echovirus, these enteroviruses enter cells with help from a shared receptor and commonly cause aseptic meningitis — which pathogens?

Coxsackievirus are a few related enteroviruses that belong to the Picornaviridae family of nonenveloped, linear, positive-sense, single-stranded, RNA viruses, as well as its genus Enterovirus, which also includes poliovirus and echovirus.
This genus of roughly 340 species includes the carnation and the sweet william, and is nicknamed 'pink' — which genus?

Dianthus (dy-) is a genus of about 340 species of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae, native mainly to Europe and Asia, with a few species in northern and southern Africa, and one species (D. repens) in arctic North America.

Dubbed 'the father of public relations' in his obituary, this Austrian-American pioneer orchestrated a famous 1929 campaign branding cigarettes as feminist 'Torches of Freedom' to encourage women to smoke — who was he?

Edward Bernays (bur-NAYZ; Austrian; November 22, 1891 March 9, 1995) was an Austrian-American pioneer in the field of public relations and propaganda, referred to in his obituary as "the father of public relations".
Co-founder of MIT's J-PAL poverty lab, she shared a 2019 Nobel with her husband and Michael Kremer for using randomized trials against global poverty — who is it?

Esther Duflo (born 25 October 1972) is a French-American economist currently serving as the Abdul Latif Jameel Professor of Poverty Alleviation and Development Economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

In English its plural is the same word for many individuals but changes form when you mean many species — a quirk of this gill-bearing, cold-blooded vertebrate that lacks limbs with digits. What is it?
Fish is an aquatic, anamniotic, gill-bearing vertebrate animal with a tough cranium to protect the brain, but lacking limbs with digits.
This field of study examines how a country's physical geography shapes its politics and its relations with other nations — what field is it?
Geopolitics (from Ancient Greek g 'earth, land' and politik 'politics') is the study of the effects of Earth's geography on politics and international relations.
A French polymath dabbling in anthropology, medicine and physics, he's best remembered for an 1895 book that became a seminal work of crowd psychology — who was he?
Gustave Le Bon (7 May 1841 - 13 December 1931) was a leading French polymath whose areas of interest included anthropology, psychology, sociology, medicine, invention, and physics.
Serving as both Reichsbank president and Minister of Economics under Hitler, this economist was credited with Germany's 1930s 'economic miracle' even as he opposed aspects of rearmament — who is he?
Hjalmar Schacht (22 January 1877 - 3 June 1970) was a German economist, banker, politician, and co-founder of the German Democratic Party.

This nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treats pain, fever, and inflammation — from migraines to arthritis — and typically starts working within an hour, whether taken orally or intravenously. What drug?
Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.
With brownish-grey fur and a pinkish-red face, this cold-hardy primate is known colloquially by a wintry nickname referencing the snow in its habitat — which species?
Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), also known as the snow monkey, is a terrestrial Old World monkey species that is native to Japan.
Brewed from the root of a Pacific pepper plant and sipped from a communal bowl in island ceremonies, this psychoactive drink takes its bitter-tasting name from Tongan and Marquesan — what is it?
Kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.
Its pale golden coat is patterned not with simple dots but with dark spots clustered into rings called rosettes, and it has prowled Africa and Asia since the Early Pleistocene — which big cat is it?
Leopard (Panthera pardus) is one of the five extant cat species in the genus Panthera.
This programming language, whose bytecode interpreter is written in ANSI C, was created in 1993 mainly to let developers extend and customize software — which language?
Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm programming language designed mainly for embedded use in applications.
Known by a nickname, this Swedish programmer created Minecraft, the best-selling video game in history, and founded the studio Mojang in 2009 — who is he?
Markus Persson (born 1 June 1979), known by the pseudonym Notch, is a Swedish video game programmer and designer.

Credited with discovering both the atmosphere of Venus and the law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions, this Russian polymath was also a poet who helped shape the modern Russian literary language and is considered a founder of modern geology — who is he?
This genus of bacteria lacks a cell wall entirely, making it naturally immune to antibiotics like penicillin that target cell-wall synthesis — name this genus?
Mycoplasma is a genus of bacteria that, like the other members of the class Mollicutes, lack a cell wall (peptidoglycan) around their cell membrane.
Doubling as a hormone, neurotransmitter, and neuromodulator, this catecholamine's very name nods to the kidney — and goes by 'noradrenaline' nearly everywhere outside the United States. What is it?

Norepinephrine (NE), also called noradrenaline (NA) or noradrenalin, is an organic chemical in the catecholamine family that functions in the brain and body as a hormone, neurotransmitter and neuromodulator.

This female reproductive gland produces eggs that travel through the oviduct to the uterus, while also functioning as an endocrine organ that secretes hormones governing the menstrual cycle — what organ is it?
Ovary (from Latin vrium 'egg') is a gonad in the female reproductive system that produces ova; when released, an ovum travels through the oviduct into the uterus.

Classically, one form of this condition wakes you at night with upper abdominal pain that eases when you eat, while another flares up after meals — and a third of older sufferers feel nothing at all. What is it?
Peptic ulcer disease refers to damage of the inner part of the stomach's gastric mucosa (lining of the stomach), the first part of the small intestine, or sometimes the lower esophagus.

Despite its fearsome reputation as a ferocious predator, this South American freshwater fish actually eats a varied diet that includes plant material, making it more omnivore than monster — what fish is it?
Piranha (or) is any of a number of freshwater fish species in the subfamily Serrasalminae, of the family Serrasalmidae, in the order Characiformes.
Including raccoons, coatis, kinkajous, and ringtails, this New World mammal family within the order Carnivora is made up mostly of omnivores — what family is it?
Procyonidae is a New World family of the order Carnivora. Procyonidae ( PROH-see-ON-i-dee) is a New World family of the order Carnivora.

This genus of roughly 1,750 flowering plant species, found worldwide mostly in temperate and mountainous regions, includes a tenacious creeping species common in European gardens as well as bulbous and meadow-dwelling relatives. What are these plants commonly called?
Ranunculus is a large genus of about 1750 species of flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae.
Caused by two strains of human herpesvirus and nicknamed 'sixth disease,' this common childhood illness brings a rapid fever that gives way to a pink rash within days — what's it called?
Roseola is an infectious disease caused by certain types of human herpes viruses.
Central nervous system depressants in this drug class are often grouped with hypnotics, though technically they're meant to calm rather than induce sleep — what class of drug is this?
Sedative is a substance that induces sedation by reducing irritability or excitement.
With the formula CH3COONa, this colorless, moisture-absorbing salt of acetic acid is deliquescent, meaning it can even dissolve in the water it pulls from the air — which compound?
Sodium acetate is a chemical compound with formula CH3COONa, also abbreviated NaOAc.

This alkaline earth metal, symbol Sr and atomic number 38, shares chemical properties with its periodic-table neighbors calcium and barium, and is mostly mined from the minerals celestine and strontianite — what element is it?
Strontium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sr and atomic number 38. The metal forms a dark oxide layer when it is exposed to air.
Known pharmaceutically as dronabinol, this is the principal psychoactive compound found in cannabis, used medically to relieve chemotherapy-induced nausea. What compound is it?
Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is a cannabinoid found in cannabis.

Stretching from the base of the skull down to the lower back and out to each shoulder blade, this large paired muscle supports the arm and moves the scapula in three distinct ways — what's the muscle?
Trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula.
Mammals, birds, amphibians, fish, and reptiles all belong to this subphylum of animals, united by a backbone and a braincase — what is it?
Vertebrate are animals with a vertebral column and a cranium.
Passed only from fathers to sons, this genetic structure carries the SRY gene that typically triggers development of male gonads in mammals — what is it?
Y chromosome is one of two sex chromosomes in therian mammals and other organisms.
Genetic in roughly 80% of cases, this long-term skin condition clogs hair follicles with dead skin and sebum, producing blackheads and pimples on the face, chest, and back — what is it?
Acne: Skin condition characterized by pimples.

German-born theoretical physicist celebrated for E=mc² and work on relativity — he won the 1921 Nobel Prize not for those breakthroughs, but for discovering the photoelectric effect. Who revolutionized physics across multiple domains?
Named for its males' mating call, which sounds like a farm animal bellowing, this large amphibian native to eastern North America has been introduced worldwide as a food source — which species?
American bullfrog: Species of amphibian. It typically inhabits large permanent water bodies such as swamps, ponds, and lakes.
Evolved from vespoid wasp ancestors in the Cretaceous, these insects are easily spotted by their elbowed antennae and slender, node-waisted bodies — what are they?
Ant: Family of insects. Nearly all ant colonies also have some fertile males called "drones" and one or more fertile females called "queens" (gynes).
Pinned by a boulder in a Utah canyon in 2003, this mountaineer amputated his own forearm with a dull pocket knife to survive, later portrayed by James Franco in a film — who is he?
Derived from a Greek word meaning 'that which is thought worthy,' which term denotes a statement accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for further reasoning?
Axiom: Statement that is taken to be true.
A colorless, sweet-smelling liquid hiding in petroleum, this ring-shaped hydrocarbon helps give gasoline its distinctive aroma — what is it?
This crested songbird in the crow family sports a black, U-shaped collar and is known for hiding acorns to eat later — which eastern North American bird?
Blue jay: Species of bird. The blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.
This rhythmic process of inhaling and exhaling delivers oxygen to the alveoli and removes carbon dioxide, with its per-minute rate counted as a vital sign — what is it?
Breathing: Process of moving air in and out of the lungs.
With the formula CaC2, this industrial compound reacts with trace moisture to give off a garlicky smell and is used to generate acetylene gas in old-fashioned lamps — what is it?
Calcium carbide: Chemical compound. Its main use industrially is in the production of acetylene and calcium cyanamide.
This mammalian order of flesh-eating species is split into cat-like and dog-like suborders, Feliformia and Caniformia, and ranks as the sixth-largest order of mammals — which order?
Carnivora: Order of mammals. Carnivora ( kar-NIV-ər-ə) is an order of placental mammals specialised primarily in eating flesh, whose members are formally referred to as carnivorans.
Known in North America as fireweed and in Britain as rosebay willowherb, this perennial flowering plant thrives across the boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere — which plant?
Chamaenerion angustifolium: Species of flowering plant in the willowherb family.

Native to Sri Lanka, the inner bark of this evergreen tree is the original source of a beloved baking spice, sometimes distinguished from a cheaper cousin as the 'true' or 'Ceylon' variety — which tree?
Cinnamomum verum: Species of tree. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this term was later generalized to include C. cassia as well.
Also known as foremilk or historically as 'beestings,' this early substance produced by mammary glands right after birth delivers antibodies and immune factors to newborns. What is it?
Colostrum: Form of milk produced immediately following the delivery of newborn.
First described in 1880 by a French neurologist, this rare delusion convinces sufferers that they are dead, don't exist, or have lost their internal organs — what is it called?
Cotard's syndrome: Delusion that one is dead or non-existent.
Bred in Germany with short legs and a long body to chase badgers into their burrows, which hound breed comes in smooth-, wire-, and long-haired varieties?
Sold as Voltaren and taken by mouth, suppository, injection, skin gel, or even eye drops, this NSAID eases pain and inflammation like gout for up to eight hours a dose — what is it?
One of the very first vertebrate apex predators on Earth, this armor-plated, jointed-neck fish patrolled open Devonian seas some 380 million years ago — which genus?
This Russian economist served as Vladimir Putin's economic adviser before becoming governor of the Central Bank of Russia — who is she?

Elvira Nabiullina: Russian economist and Governor of the Bank of Russia. Elvira Sakhipzadovna Nabiullina (born 29 October 1963) is a Russian economist and current governor of the Central Bank of Russia.
This branch of anthropology studies individual cultures through participant observation, with roots in early 20th-century social science — what is this field called?
Ethnography: Systematic study of people and cultures.
First described from a skull in 1846 and initially mistaken for a porpoise, this highly social oceanic dolphin gets its common name from a skull resembling that of the orca — which species?
False killer whale: Species of oceanic dolphin in the genus Pseudorca.
Also nicknamed 'muscae volitantes' — Latin for flying flies — these tiny shadowy specks drift across your vision, especially noticeable against a blank blue sky. What are they?
Floater: Deposits within the eye's vitreous humour.
Bound together by gravity, this vast system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter can range from a dwarf with under a thousand stars to a supergiant with a hundred trillion — what is it?
Galaxy: System of stars and interstellar matter. The word is derived from the Greek galaxias (γαλαξίας), meaning 'milky', a reference to the Milky Way galaxy that contains the Solar System.
The last survivor of an order that first appeared over 290 million years ago, this long-lived East Asian tree with unique fan-shaped leaves is celebrated as a living fossil — what is it?
Ginkgo biloba: Species of tree. Fossils similar to the living species, belonging to the genus Ginkgo, extend back to the Middle Jurassic epoch about 170 million years ago.
Also known as the Congo variety, this African bird in the family Psittacidae lost its old 'African' nickname once a related Timneh species was split off as its own species — what is it?
Grown as deciduous shrubs across the temperate Northern Hemisphere and related to the birch family, this plant produces a popular round brown nut — which plant genus?
This branch of biology studies the microscopic structure of tissues, historically distinguished from cytology (the study of cells) and organology (the study of organs) — what is it called?
Histology: Study of the microscopic anatomy of cells and tissues of plants and animals.
A yellow-flowered perennial whose leaves look perforated by translucent glands, this plant is famed in folklore and traditional medicine under a saintly common name — what is its botanical name?
Hypericum perforatum: Flowering plant in the St John's wort family.
Endemic to semiarid central-eastern Australia and also called the "fierce snake," this elapid was rediscovered in 1972 after nearly 90 years of obscurity — what is it?
Inland taipan: Extremely venomous snake native to Australia.
The first woman to chair the Federal Reserve, this American economist later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — who is she?
Janet Yellen: American economist and government official (born 1946)
Also known as the English or Persian walnut, this tree species native to Eurasia is cultivated worldwide, with China as its leading producer today — what is it?
Juglans regia: Species of tree (walnut). Juglans regia, known by various common names including the common walnut, English walnut, or Persian walnut amongst other names, is a species of walnut.

Ranked alongside Aristotle and Frege among history's most significant logicians, this thinker proved his completeness theorem in his 1929 Vienna dissertation before publishing his famous incompleteness theorems two years later — who is he?
Kurt Gödel: Mathematical logician and philosopher.
Often called the last physicist to master every branch of the field, this Soviet scientist co-discovered the density matrix method and developed the theory of superfluidity — who is he?
Nicknamed the sea devil, frogfish, or fishing frog, this species anchors a major commercial fishery in the Irish Sea and ranges from the Barents Sea to the Mediterranean — which fish?
Lophius piscatorius: Species of fish. Lophius piscatorius, commonly known as the angler, toadfish, sea frog, fishing frog, frogfish, or sea devil, is a species of Lophius in the family Lophiidae.
Males of this widespread dabbling duck species sport iridescent green heads, while females have brown-speckled plumage — which bird?
Mallard: Species of duck. The mallard or wild duck (Anas platyrhynchos) is a dabbling duck that breeds throughout the temperate and subtropical Americas, Eurasia, and North Africa.
Distinguished by its darker camouflage, conformal fuel tanks, and a two-seat cockpit, this all-weather multirole fighter first flew in 1986 for long-range interdiction missions — what is it?
McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle: American all-weather multirole fighter aircraft.

Born from the French Revolution's push to standardize units into the metric system, this scientific field oversees everything from the SI unit system to the labs that keep rulers honest — what is it called?
Metrology: Science of measurement and its application.
Making up about 23% of all named marine organisms, this phylum is the second-largest in the animal kingdom after the arthropods — what is it?
This condition describes an abnormally dilated pupil that remains enlarged even in bright light, often triggered by trauma, disease, or certain drugs — what is it called?
Mydriasis: Excessive dilation of the pupil.
This 17th-century Dane was a pioneer of both anatomy and geology — he doubted that fossils "grew" in the ground — before becoming a Catholic bishop and being beatified by the Church. Who was he?
Nicolas Steno: Danish scientist and Catholic bishop (1638 – 1686)
This order of predatory flying insects includes dragonflies and damselflies, whose aquatic larvae are voracious carnivores capable of overpowering small fish and tadpoles — what is it called?
Odonata: Order of insects that includes the dragonflies and damselflies. The adults are superb aerial hunters and their legs are specialised for catching prey in flight.

Powered by NADH and FADH₂ handed off from glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, this mitochondrial pathway is how nearly all aerobic organisms produce ATP — far more efficiently than fermentation. What's it called?
Oxidative phosphorylation: Metabolic pathway. Oxidative phosphorylation uses these molecules and O2 to produce ATP, which is used throughout the cell whenever energy is needed.
The males of this pheasant-family bird are famed for piercing calls and extravagant plumage; its Asiatic, green, and Congo species span India to central Africa — what common name covers them all?
Peafowl: Group of large game birds.
This anxiety disorder involves an irrational, excessive fear that persists more than six months and can trigger fainting in blood-or-injury cases — what is it?
Phobia: Anxiety disorder classified by a persistent and excessive fear of an object or situation.
Downgraded from planet to dwarf in 2006 when astronomers adopted a new definition, this Kuiper belt object orbits beyond Neptune—what celestial body is it?
Pluto: Largest dwarf planet. Pluto (minor-planet number 134340) is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Sold under the brand name Phenergan, this first-generation antihistamine treats allergies and nausea but has also seen recreational misuse alongside codeine — which drug?
Promethazine: Sedating antihistamine. Promethazine is taken by mouth (oral), as a rectal suppository, or by injection into a muscle (IM).
Once one of America's leading rocket experts with an MIT aeronautics degree, he was deported to China in 1955 and went on to father that nation's space program — which aerospace engineer?

Nicknamed the 'Jug,' this WWII American fighter-bomber carried eight .50-caliber machine guns and weighed up to eight tons fully loaded, making it one of the heaviest fighters of the war — which aircraft?

Republic P-47 Thunderbolt: Family of fighter aircraft. The Republic P-47 Thunderbolt (nicknamed the "Jug") is a World War II-era fighter aircraft produced by the American company Republic Aviation from 1941 through 1945.

A Mediterranean shrub in the mint family, this plant bears fragrant, needle-like evergreen leaves and purple, white, pink, or blue flowers — and those leaves are a beloved cooking flavoring. What is it?
Rosemary: Species of plant. It has numerous cultivars, and its leaves are commonly used as a flavoring.
This Indian-American executive became CEO of a major tech company in 2014, succeeding Steve Ballmer, after leading its cloud and enterprise division — who is he?
This Pakistani-American billionaire owns an NFL franchise and a Premier League club, made his fortune supplying auto parts, and backs a wrestling promotion run by his son — who is he?
Shahid Khan: Pakistani and American businessman (born 1950)
Known commonly as chlorine bleach when dissolved in water, this unstable inorganic compound decomposes to release chlorine gas — what is it?
Sodium hypochlorite: Chemical compound. Sodium hypochlorite is an alkaline inorganic chemical compound with the formula NaOCl (also written as NaClO).
This physics law states that a black body's radiated energy per unit area is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature — which law?
Stefan–Boltzmann law: Physical law on the emissive power of black body.
Time named this marine biologist its first "Hero for the Planet" in 1998, the same year she became a National Geographic Explorer — and she'd already been NOAA's first chief scientist. Who is she?
Sylvia Earle: American marine biologist and lecturer.
Developed under the codename 'WhiteStar' and unveiled in Hawthorne, California in 2009, this full-size electric sedan won Motor Trend's Car of the Year in 2013 — which car?
Tesla Model S: Battery-electric full-size car. The Tesla Model S is a battery-electric, four-door full-size car that was produced by the American automaker Tesla from 2012 to 2026.
Commonly called jock itch, this contagious fungal infection of the groin and buttocks causes an intensely itchy, red, scaly rash with a well-defined curved border — what is it?
Tinea cruris: Fungal infection. It is often associated with athlete's foot and fungal nail infections, excessive sweating, and sharing of infected towels or sports clothing.
Named after the Turkish word for turban, which it was thought to resemble, this spring-blooming bulb belongs to the lily family and includes about 75 species — which flower?
This abnormal enlargement of veins in the scrotum is the most common correctable cause of male infertility, affecting around 15% of all men — what is it called?
Varicocele: Abnormal enlargement of the pampiniform plexus veins in the scrotum.

Also known as 'wet brain,' this neurological condition results from a severe thiamine deficiency and classically presents with confusion, poor coordination, and eye movement problems — which condition is it?
Wernicke encephalopathy: Medical condition. The condition is part of a larger group of thiamine deficiency disorders that includes beriberi, in all its forms, and alcoholic Korsakoff syndrome.
This Egyptian archaeologist twice served as his country's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities and has dug at sites from the Nile Delta to the Western Desert — who is he?
What is the chemical symbol for bromine?
The symbol for bromine is Br. Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.
Tantalum is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for tantalum is Ta. Tantalum is a chemical element; it has symbol Ta and atomic number 73.

In what year was Donald Sutherland born?
Donald Sutherland: Donald McNichol Sutherland (17 July 1935 – 20 June 2024) was a Canadian actor.
In what year was Emma Stone born?
Emma Stone: Emily Jean "Emma" Stone (born November 6, 1988) is an American actress and film producer.
In what year was Jennifer Garner born?
Jennifer Garner: Jennifer Anne Garner (born April 17, 1972) is an American actress.
In what year was Hayden Christensen born?
Hayden Christensen (born April 19, 1981) is a Canadian actor.
In what year was America Ferrera born?
America Ferrera: America Georgina Ferrera (born April 18, 1984) is an American actress, director and television producer.
In what year was Priscilla Presley born?
